message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"12.26","text":"And I answered, “Does it not seem to you, then, that even the innkeeper is humane, since she benefited a female stranger whom she did not know?” Peter replied, “I know that I can call her merciful, but I do not dare call her humane, since I would not even call a mother child-loving; for she has been persuaded to cherish her child by labor pains and upbringing. Just as the lover is flattered by familiarity and by the bed, and the friend by reciprocation, so also the merciful person is moved by misfortune. Still, the merciful person is close to the humane person, because he is moved to do good without hunting for anything to receive. In this respect, then, he is humane.” And I said, “By what actions, then, can someone be humane?” Peter answered, “Since I see that you are eager to hear what an act of humaneness actually is, I will not hesitate to tell you. Humane is the person who does good even to enemies. Hear why this is so. Humaneness is male-and-female: its female part is called mercy, while its male part has been named love for one’s neighbor. Every human being is a human being’s neighbor, not merely some particular human being; for the evil person and the good person, the enemy and the friend, are all human beings. Therefore, the person who practices humaneness must imitate God, doing good to the righteous and the unrighteous, just as God himself provides everyone in the present world with both his sun and his rains. But if you wish to do good to the good and no longer to the evil, or even to punish them, you are attempting to perform the work of a judge; you are not striving to possess humaneness.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"φιλάνθρωπος","chosen":"humane","rationale":"The term denotes active benevolence toward human beings. “Humane” preserves its connection with the recurring noun “humaneness” without importing the modern institutional sense of “philanthropic.”"},{"source_quote":"οὔτε τὴν τεκοῦσαν φιλότεκνον","chosen":"I would not even call a mother child-loving","rationale":"The verb “call” is supplied from the preceding εἰπεῖν/λέγειν. More literally, τὴν τεκοῦσαν is “the woman who gave birth.”"},{"source_quote":"ἄνευ τοῦ τι θηρᾶσθαι λαβεῖν","chosen":"without hunting for anything to receive","rationale":"This retains the source’s hunting image and the expectation of receiving some benefit in return."},{"source_quote":"φιλανθρωπία ἐστὶν ἀρρενόθηλυς","chosen":"Humaneness is male-and-female","rationale":"ἀρρενόθηλυς explicitly combines the male and female categories; the unusual image is preserved rather than normalized as merely “twofold.”"},{"source_quote":"τὸ θῆλυ μέρος ἐλεημοσύνη λέγεται","chosen":"its female part is called mercy","rationale":"Here ἐλεημοσύνη continues the preceding language of showing mercy. “Almsgiving” is possible elsewhere but would narrow this context unnecessarily."},{"source_quote":"πλησίον δὲ ἀνθρώπῳ ἐστὶν ὁ πᾶς ἄνθρωπος, οὐχ ὁ τὶς ἄνθρωπος","chosen":"Every human being is a human being’s neighbor, not merely some particular human being","rationale":"The rendering preserves the contrast between all humanity and an individually restricted class of neighbors."},{"source_quote":"κακοὺς δὲ μηκέτι ἢ καὶ κολάζειν","chosen":"and no longer to the evil, or even to punish them","rationale":"The omitted repetition of “do good” is supplied from the preceding clause, while μηκέτι and the escalation introduced by ἢ καί are retained."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"12.27","text":"And I said, “Surely God too, since he is going to judge at that time, as you teach us, is not humane?” Peter replied, “You are saying the opposite. It is precisely because he will judge that he is humane. For in loving and showing mercy to those who have been wronged, he punishes those who wronged them.” And I said, “Therefore, if I too do good to the good but punish those who commit injustice to the extent that they have wronged human beings, am I humane?” Peter answered, “If, along with possessing foreknowledge, you also possessed authority to judge, you would rightly do this: because you had received the authority, you would condemn those whom God created; and because of your foreknowledge, you would judge without error, acquitting some as righteous and condemning others as unrighteous.” And I said, “You have spoken correctly and truthfully, for it is impossible for someone who lacks foreknowledge to judge correctly. Sometimes people appear to be good while secretly committing unlawful acts, while at other times good people are considered evil because of their enemies’ slander. But even if someone possesses authority to torture and interrogate and then passes judgment, it would not even then be possible for him to judge justly in every case. For some who were murderers endured the tortures and were released as innocent, while others who were innocent failed to endure the tortures, falsely accused themselves, and were punished as guilty.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"Τοὐναντίον λέγεις","chosen":"You are saying the opposite","rationale":"The expression directly reverses Clement’s inference; it need not be expanded into a theological explanation."},{"source_quote":"καθὸ ἀνθρώπους ἠδίκησαν","chosen":"to the extent that they have wronged human beings","rationale":"ἀνθρώπους is read as the object of ἠδίκησαν and καθό as “to the extent that.” A less likely alternative is “insofar as, being human, they did wrong.”"},{"source_quote":"διὰ μὲν τὸ εἰληφέναι τὴν ἐξουσίαν καταδικάζων οὓς ὁ θεὸς ἐδημιούργησεν","chosen":"because you had received the authority, you would condemn those whom God created","rationale":"The participle καταδικάζων describes how the hypothetical judging would be performed. The striking reference to condemning God’s creatures is retained."},{"source_quote":"οὓς μὲν ὡς δικαίους δικαιῶν","chosen":"acquitting some as righteous","rationale":"In this judicial context δικαιόω means to declare someone righteous or acquit, rather than to make that person morally righteous."},{"source_quote":"οὐδὲ οὕτως τὸ πάντως δικαίως αὐτῷ δικάσαι ἐγίνετο","chosen":"it would not even then be possible for him to judge justly in every case","rationale":"πάντως is taken distributively as “in every case.” “Altogether justly” is also lexically possible but is less precise in the examples that follow."},{"source_quote":"ἑαυτῶν καταψευσάμενοι ὡς αἴτιοι","chosen":"falsely accused themselves ... as guilty","rationale":"καταψεύδομαι with the reflexive means to testify falsely against oneself; αἴτιοι here denotes responsibility or guilt."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"12.28","text":"And Peter said, “These points are moderately sound, but hear the greater one. When some people sin or act well, among the things they now do some are their own and others belong to someone else; yet it is just for each person to be punished for his own sins or benefited for his own right actions. But it is impossible for anyone except a prophet alone, who possesses foreknowledge, to know which of the things done by someone are his own and which were not; for everything that happens through him is seen.” And I said, “I would like to learn how, among acts of injustice or right actions, some are one’s own and others belong to someone else.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"Μετρίως ... ἔχει καὶ ταῦτα","chosen":"These points are moderately sound","rationale":"μετρίως gives qualified approval rather than complete endorsement. “These things are reasonable to a degree” is an alternative."},{"source_quote":"ἃ μὲν ἴδια αὐτῶν ἐστίν, ἃ δὲ ἀλλότρια","chosen":"some are their own and others belong to someone else","rationale":"ἴδια and ἀλλότρια contrast actions attributable to the person with actions whose true ownership or agency lies elsewhere."},{"source_quote":"ἐπὶ τοῖς ἰδίοις κατορθώμασιν εὐεργετεῖσθαι","chosen":"benefited for his own right actions","rationale":"κατόρθωμα denotes a right, successful, or virtuous action. “Achievements” is possible but could obscure the moral contrast with sins."},{"source_quote":"πλὴν προφήτῃ μόνῳ πρόγνωσιν ἔχοντι","chosen":"except a prophet alone, who possesses foreknowledge","rationale":"Both the exception expressed by πλήν and the exclusivity of μόνῳ are retained."},{"source_quote":"ποῖά, ἐστιν αὐτοῦ ἴδια, ποῖα δὲ οὐχ ἦν","chosen":"which ... are his own and which were not","rationale":"The translation preserves the supplied shift from present ἐστιν to past ἦν. The latter could refer to actions that were not originally the person’s own; regularizing it to a present tense would require emendation."},{"source_quote":"πάντα γὰρ δι’ αὐτοῦ γινόμενα βλέπεται","chosen":"for everything that happens through him is seen","rationale":"διά with the genitive is represented as “through,” preserving the distinction between apparent agency and ultimate ownership. “Everything done through him appears” is also possible."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ποῖά, ἐστιν αὐτοῦ ἴδια, ποῖα δὲ οὐχ ἦν","issue":"The shift from present ἐστιν to past ἦν is abrupt, and the printed comma after ποῖά is editorially awkward. The supplied wording nevertheless permits a defensible rendering without changing the Greek.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"12.29","text":"And Peter answered, “The prophet of the truth said, ‘The good things must come; blessed, however, is the one through whom they come. Likewise, the evil things must necessarily come; but woe to the one through whom they come.’ Now if evil things come through evil people and good things are borne through good people, there must belong to each person what is his own—being good or evil—also as a result of the things he did beforehand, through the coming of the subsequent good or evil things. These, being his own by choice, have been arranged by God’s providence to pass through him. For this, then, is God’s judgment: just as in a contest, the one who has passed through every hardship and been found blameless is to be deemed worthy of eternal life. For those who, by their own resolve, have advanced in goodness are tested by those who, by their own resolve, have persisted in evil: they are persecuted, hated, reviled, plotted against, beaten, exploited, slandered, pressed into service, and abused, suffering all those things through which becoming angry and rushing to retaliation seem reasonably to arise.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὰ ἀγαθὰ ἐλθεῖν δεῖ, μακάριος δὲ (φησίν) δι’ οὗ ἔρχεται","chosen":"The good things must come; blessed, however, is the one through whom they come","rationale":"The positive saying is translated exactly as supplied and is not harmonized with a more familiar form of a similar saying."},{"source_quote":"τὰ κακὰ ἀνάγκη ἐλθεῖν, οὐαὶ δὲ δι’ οὗ ἔρχεται","chosen":"the evil things must necessarily come; but woe to the one through whom they come","rationale":"ἀνάγκη conveys necessity. The singular Greek verb treats the neuter plural collectively; natural English uses the plural “they come.”"},{"source_quote":"προσεῖναι δεῖ ἑκάστῳ τὸ ἴδιον (τὸ ἀγαθὸν εἶναι ἢ κακόν) καὶ ἐξ ὧν προέπραξεν","chosen":"there must belong to each person what is his own—being good or evil—also as a result of the things he did beforehand","rationale":"The parenthesis identifies the person’s own characteristic as being good or evil. The attachment of καὶ ἐξ ὧν προέπραξεν is compressed; it may alternatively mean “and [this is known] from what he previously did.”"},{"source_quote":"ἅτινα ἴδια αὐτοῦ τῆς αἱρέσεως ὄντα","chosen":"These, being his own by choice","rationale":"αἵρεσις here is understood as personal choice or resolve. The genitive construction is compact and could also be rendered “belonging to his own choice.”"},{"source_quote":"ὑπὸ τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ προνοίας διελθεῖν ᾠκονόμηται","chosen":"have been arranged by God’s providence to pass through him","rationale":"The subject is taken from the preceding good or evil things, while “through him” is supplied from the established διὰ κακῶν/δι’ ἀγαθῶν framework. An alternative is “to come upon him,” but that weakens the repeated idea of events passing through agents."},{"source_quote":"ἐπεὶ οὖν κρίσις αὕτη θεῷ","chosen":"For this, then, is God’s judgment","rationale":"The clause is treated as a nominal statement introducing the content expressed by the following accusative and infinitive. More formally, it could be “Since, then, this judgment belongs to God.”"},{"source_quote":"ἀγγαρευόμενοι","chosen":"pressed into service","rationale":"The verb denotes being compelled to perform service or labor; the coercive force is retained."},{"source_quote":"πρὸς ἄμυναν ὁρμᾶν","chosen":"rushing to retaliation","rationale":"ἄμυνα may denote defense or retaliatory action. “Retaliation” fits the following prohibition against answering mistreatment in kind, while “self-defense” remains possible."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"οἱ γὰρ ἐν ἀγαθοῖς ἰδίᾳ βουλῇ προκύψαντες;","issue":"The printed Greek semicolon functions as a question mark, but the clause continues directly with ὑπὸ τῶν ... πειράζονται and is syntactically declarative. It is treated as anomalous editorial punctuation, not as a gap or missing wording.","proposed_reading":"οἱ γὰρ ἐν ἀγαθοῖς ἰδίᾳ βουλῇ προκύψαντες,","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"ἐπεὶ οὖν κρίσις αὕτη θεῷ, ὥσπερ ἐπ᾽ ἀγῶνος τὸν διὰ πάσης κακουχίας διεληλυθότα καὶ ἄμεμπτον εὑρεθέντα, ἐκεῖνον ζωῆς αἰωνίου καταξιοῦσθαι —·","issue":"The construction is compressed, with a nominal statement followed by an accusative-and-infinitive formulation, and the supplied closing dash and point are editorially unusual. A defensible sense is available without restoring or omitting words.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"12.30","text":"But the Teacher, knowing that those who do these things unjustly stand condemned because of earlier sins, and that through condemned people the spirit of evil carries out these things, advised them, as people practicing humaneness, to have mercy on the human beings insofar as they are human beings and become instruments of evil through sin. He also advised them, insofar as it lay with them, although they were being wronged, to release the wrongdoers from condemnation, so that they might help them as sober people help the drunk—with prayers, fasts, and blessings, neither resisting nor retaliating—so that they would not force them to sin still more. For when suffering has in any event been decreed for someone, it is not reasonable for him to be indignant with the person through whom the suffering comes, when he reflects that even if that person had not mistreated him, because he was in any event going to be mistreated, his suffering would have come through another. Why, then, am I indignant with the person who treated me this way, when it has in any event been decreed that I suffer? Moreover, if on the pretext of retaliation we do the same things to the evil, then we who are good do the same thing as the evil, except that we are second rather than first. And, as I said, one should not be indignant, knowing that by God’s providence the evil punish the good. Those, therefore, who are angry with those who punish them sin as people who insult God’s emissaries; whereas those who honor them and treat them in ways opposite to how people regarded as wrongdoers are treated show reverence toward God, who has so determined.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"διὰ καταδίκων τὸ τῆς κακίας πνεῦμα ταῦτα ἐνεργεῖ","chosen":"through condemned people the spirit of evil carries out these things","rationale":"The condemned people are represented as the intermediate agents through whom the spirit acts; this claim is preserved without theological harmonization."},{"source_quote":"τοὺς μὲν ἀνθρώπους καθὰ ἄνθρωποί εἰσιν ... ἐλεεῖν συνεβούλευσεν, ὡς φιλανθρωπίαν ἀσκοῦσιν","chosen":"advised them, as people practicing humaneness, to have mercy on the human beings insofar as they are human beings","rationale":"ἀσκοῦσιν is read as a dative plural participle referring to the implicitly advised hearers. It could formally be read as a finite verb, but that would leave its relation to ὡς and συνεβούλευσεν less clear."},{"source_quote":"καὶ δι᾽ ἁμαρτίας ὄργανα γινομένους κακίας","chosen":"and become instruments of evil through sin","rationale":"κακίας is taken with ὄργανα, while δι᾽ ἁμαρτίας identifies the means by which people become such instruments."},{"source_quote":"τὸ ὅσον ἐπ᾽ αὐτοῖς ἐστίν","chosen":"insofar as it lay with them","rationale":"The idiom limits their responsibility to what is within their power. “As far as depended on them” is a more literal alternative."},{"source_quote":"ὥσπερ οἱ νήφοντες τοῖς μεθύουσιν βοηθῶσιν","chosen":"as sober people help the drunk","rationale":"Because the source explicitly contrasts νήφοντες with μεθύουσιν, the literal drunk-versus-sober image is retained rather than using the more general “clear-minded.”"},{"source_quote":"τοῦ γὰρ παθεῖν πάντως κεκριμένου τινί","chosen":"when suffering has in any event been decreed for someone","rationale":"πάντως is understood as inevitability in this context. The genitive absolute establishes the condition under which indignation is judged unreasonable."},{"source_quote":"τί οὖν ἀγανακτῶ τῷ διαθεμένῳ","chosen":"Why, then, am I indignant with the person who treated me this way","rationale":"διατίθημι here refers elliptically to the person’s hostile treatment. “The person who dealt with me” is a more literal alternative."},{"source_quote":"παρὰ τὸ πρῶτοι δεύτεροι","chosen":"except that we are second rather than first","rationale":"The compressed contrast means that the good repeat the same conduct but do so responsively rather than initiating it."},{"source_quote":"ὡς τοὺς ἀποστόλους θεοῦ ὑβρίζοντες","chosen":"as people who insult God’s emissaries","rationale":"ἀπόστολοι is generic here for persons sent or used as agents, not necessarily the particular apostolic office; “messengers” is also possible."},{"source_quote":"τὰ ἐναντία τοῖς ἀδικεῖν νομιζομένοις διατιθέμενοι αὐτοὺς","chosen":"treat them in ways opposite to how people regarded as wrongdoers are treated","rationale":"τοῖς ... νομιζομένοις is taken as masculine and as the comparison governed by ἐναντία. A viable alternative takes it as neuter: “treat them with the opposites of things considered injurious.”"},{"source_quote":"εἰς τὸν θεὸν τὸν οὕτω βουλευσάμενον εὐσεβοῦσιν","chosen":"show reverence toward God, who has so determined","rationale":"βουλεύομαι is understood as resolving or determining the providential arrangement. “Who has planned it this way” is also possible."}],"source_issues":[]}]}
